web_evidence.title: Narratological and Artistic Analysis of Khaled Hossieni’s A Thousand Splendid Suns
web_evidence.note: The scholarly narratological analysis explicitly identifies third-person narration and an anonymous heterodiegetic narrator who is not a character in the story.

web_evidence.title: A Thousand Splendid Suns Study Guide
web_evidence.note: The guide explicitly describes the whole novel as third person, with focalization alternating between Mariam and Laila while the narrator remains outside both characters.

web_evidence.title: A Thousand Splendid Suns Novel Units Sample
web_evidence.note: The educational publisher's guide explicitly lists the novel's point of view as third-person omniscient.

web_evidence.title: A Thousand Splendid Suns by Khaled Hosseini
web_evidence.note: The publisher-hosted author interview confirms the novel's dual perspective and identifies the title verse as a translated poem used within a scene; it supports the structural interpretation but does not itself name the grammatical person.

web_evidence.title: A Thousand Splendid Suns Reading Group Guide
web_evidence.note: Bloomsbury's guide reproduces short passages from the opening and several interior pages that consistently present Mariam and Laila in third person.

search_log: Searched "A Thousand Splendid Suns Khaled Hosseini excerpt publisher" and opened the author, Penguin Random House, and Bloomsbury pages; the author site's excerpt link redirected to a PRH Look Inside interface without accessible sustained sample text.
Searched "A Thousand Splendid Suns point of view third person narrator scholarly" and opened two journal analyses, LitCharts, and publisher-produced teaching materials.
Searched "A Thousand Splendid Suns first chapter excerpt Mariam third person" and verified Bloomsbury's opening sentence and additional short interior passages.
Searched "A Thousand Splendid Suns alternating point of view Mariam Laila third person"; credible sources consistently described alternating focalization within third-person narration.

Searched the title with "epistolary," "diary," "frame narrative," "first person narration," "second person narration," and "multiple narrators"; no credible evidence of sustained first- or second-person base sections emerged. A few low-quality generic PDFs mislabeled the narration as first person, but their assertions conflict with the primary-text passages and explicit scholarly analysis.
person_note: The controlling narrator is anonymous, nonparticipating, and third person. Focalization shifts between Mariam and Laila, but this is not ALTERNATING because the grammatical person remains third throughout those sections. Sustained event quotations q01433, q01439, q01440, and q01449 independently expose external narration, agreeing with the scholarly whole-book analysis and explicit reference guides. First- and second-person pronouns elsewhere belong to dialogue, maxims, or the embedded title poem. No material conflict remains; the only uncertainty concerns isolated or clipped quotations that cannot establish person on their own.
